subject: Civil Engineering
title: Grain Size: Sand, Silt, and Clay
description: Learn Grain Size: Sand, Silt, and Clay in one minute.

hook.text: A grain of sand is visible. A clay particle is 1,000 times smaller — invisible.

buildup.text: Sand grains are gritty and drain fast. Silt is smooth. Clay is sticky when wet.

discovery.text: Grain size determines everything — drainage, strength, and compressibility.

twist.text: Clay particles are flat plates that attract water — that's why clay swells and shrinks.

climax.text: A sieve analysis sorts grains by size to classify the soil for engineering use.

punchline.text: The tiniest grains cause the biggest problems.

quiz.question: Why does clay swell when wet and shrink when dry?
options: Clay contains air pockets that expand with moisture
Clay particles are flat plates that attract and absorb water between layers
Chemical reactions in clay produce gas when exposed to water

details.summary: Soil particles range from boulders and gravel through sand and silt down to microscopic clay particles smaller than 0.002 millimeters. Grain size determines fundamental behavior: coarse-grained soils drain freely and derive strength from friction between particles.
details.whyItMatters: Grain size is the primary indicator of how soil will behave under load and with water. A soil's drainage, strength, compressibility, and frost susceptibility all correlate strongly with particle size distribution.
takeaways: Gravel and sand are coarse-grained soils that drain freely and resist loads by friction
Silt and clay are fine-grained soils that drain slowly and may be highly compressible
Clay particles smaller than 0.002 mm have surface charges that control their behavior

faq.question: Why do clay particles behave so differently from sand particles?
faq.answer: Clay particles are flat, plate-like minerals with electrically charged surfaces that attract water molecules. These surface forces dominate behavior at such small scale, making clay plastic, cohesive, and nearly impermeable.

faq.question: How is particle size distribution measured in the laboratory?
faq.answer: Coarse particles are separated by passing soil through a series of wire mesh sieves of decreasing size. Fine particles below 0.075 mm are measured by hydrometer analysis, which tracks how fast particles settle in a water column based on Stokes' Law.
